subtype: Approach: defining a minimum viable version first [Thinking]
passage: In the school library in Auckland, Mateo, Mei and a third friend stared at a whiteboard covered in ideas: accounts, star ratings, comments, a forum, dark mode. “We have four weeks and one laptop,” Mei said. “What does someone need on day one?” Mateo thought aloud. “A student wants last year's notes. That's all. One page, PDFs sorted by subject.” “No login?” “No login. If people use it, we add ratings later. If nobody does, at least we didn't build a forum for no one.” Mei rubbed out every item except PDFs by subject and drew a box round it. By Friday they had uploaded twelve files into six folders, and the whole site fit on one page.

qa.q: How many files did the group upload by Friday?
qa.a: Twelve files in six folders.

qa.q: What might Mei be feeling as Mei rubs out the list?
qa.a: Relieved and focused: the smaller target makes the four weeks look manageable.

qa.q: What else could the group do to decide what to add next, and why?
qa.a: Ask classmates what they miss after using the first version, since real users show which extras matter.

qa.q: How does the plan look to a student who just wants last year's notes?
qa.a: That student gets what they need straight away and does not care about ratings or a forum yet.

grounding: A group decides that the first version of a notes site is just uploaded PDFs sorted by subject, leaving accounts and ratings for later.

subtype: Approach: task decomposition and dividing roles [Action]
passage: When our teacher asked for a website for the science fair, I secretly planned to do the whole thing myself, because I didn't trust anyone else to do it right. Then Tanvir opened a shared sheet and said, “Let's split it.” Three columns went up: design, content, coding. Prisha took design, due on the 15th. I took content, due the 18th. Tanvir took coding, due the 22nd. We agreed to meet for ten minutes on Tuesdays and Fridays at lunch to say what was done and what was stuck. I nearly argued about who got coding. On the 20th the site went live, two days early, and none of us had stayed up all night. — Jyoti

qa.q: How often did the team meet?
qa.a: Twice a week for ten minutes, on Tuesdays and Fridays.

qa.q: How did Jyoti feel at first about splitting the work?
qa.a: Reluctant and distrustful: Jyoti had secretly planned to do everything because of not trusting the others to get it right.

qa.q: What could the team do if one person fell behind, and why?
qa.a: Raise it at the ten-minute meeting and move a small piece to someone else, since early notice keeps the deadline safe.

qa.q: How does the plan look to Tanvir, who took coding?
qa.a: Tanvir gets a clear, named job with a date, so there is no guessing about what the others expect.

grounding: Three teens split a website into design, content and coding, write who does what by when and check progress twice a week.

subtype: Approach: using free tools within constraints [Thinking]
passage: Parveen had empty pockets and no bank card, which ruled out most website tools. The first evening was grim. Then Parveen made a list. “Free builder and free hosting: fine. No video plugins, no shop. So what can a free site do that a paid one doesn't? Nothing special. Unless the content is better.” The project became a guide to the birds of the neighbourhood park, with careful photos and short, accurate notes on each one. Minakshi, a classmate, looked at the first page and asked, “Won't it look plain?” Parveen shrugged. “Plain is the rule now. Big pictures, clear names, nothing that slows down a phone.” It was a limit, and it decided the whole design.

qa.q: Why did Parveen choose a free site builder?
qa.a: Parveen had empty pockets and no bank card.

qa.q: What might Parveen feel about having fewer features?
qa.a: Accepting and a little proud: the limit became a design rule instead of a complaint.

qa.q: What else could Parveen do to use the limits well, and why?
qa.a: Ask a few readers whether the bird notes are clear and easy to read on a phone, since good content is the site's strength.

qa.q: How does the site look to Minakshi?
qa.a: Minakshi worries that it will look plain, but the clear names and large pictures help visitors find what they need quickly.

grounding: With no money and no card, a teen picks free tools, accepts fewer features and puts effort into content quality.

subtype: Approach: testing with real users early [Action]
passage:
“Don't help me, Kavitha Masi. Just use it,” Naveen said, and held out the tablet.
“Where are the idli recipes?”
“Try finding them.”
Kavitha Masi tapped the screen twice. “There's just three little lines. Is that a menu?”
“It's the menu button.”
Cousin Pallavi peered over. “I thought that was decoration.”
Four of the five relatives around the dining table couldn't find the recipe list. Naveen said nothing and wrote in his notebook: menu unclear, 4 of 5. His hand itched to point at it.
Later he said, “Nobody's getting new photos until the menu says Recipes in words.”
Pallavi laughed. “Finally, someone tests a blog before making it pretty.”

qa.q: How many of the five relatives could not find the recipe list?
qa.a: Four of the five.

qa.q: How might Naveen have felt while watching the relatives struggle?
qa.a: Nervous and a little disappointed but curious: he held back from helping even though his hand itched to point.

qa.q: What could Naveen do after fixing the menu, and why?
qa.a: Test again with a different set of people, since a fix that works for these five may still confuse others.

qa.q: How does the site look to Kavitha Masi?
qa.a: Kavitha Masi found it confusing instead of pretty, so she would want the menu to say clearly where the recipes are.

grounding: A student shows a rough recipe blog to five relatives, watches where they get lost and fixes the menu first.

subtype: Approach: overbuilding features before anyone uses it [Pitfall]
passage: I wanted my timetable app to be perfect before anyone saw it. So I added chat. Then badges. Then a dark mode, because a good app has one. Every evening there was one more thing, and I told myself I was almost done. But my exam-free weeks ran out, and the app never went live. Later my friend Simran told me what the class had actually wanted: a plain page with the timetable on it, something to open on the way to school. A photo of the timetable would have done the job. I had spent six weeks on features that nobody had asked for and forgotten to ask anyone what they needed. — Rashmi

qa.q: What had the class actually wanted?
qa.a: A plain page with the timetable on it.

qa.q: How does Rashmi feel looking back?
qa.a: Regretful and a bit embarrassed at spending six weeks on features nobody asked for.

qa.q: What could Rashmi have done instead, and why?
qa.a: Share a plain timetable page first and add features only when classmates ask, because real requests show what is worth building.

qa.q: How does the situation look to Simran?
qa.a: Simran, who knew what the class wanted, saw the extras as unnecessary and probably wished Rashmi had asked earlier.

grounding: A teen adds chat, badges and dark mode before sharing, runs out of exam-free weeks and launches nothing.

subtype: Approach: pre-mortem on why the project might die [Thinking]
passage: Before writing a line of code, Lokesh's team of four sat on the terrace and did something odd. “It's April,” said Lakshmi. “The project is dead. Why?” They wrote fast on sticky notes: exams, nobody checked in, one person doing all the work, the thing got boring, someone lost the password. Lokesh read them out. Some were funny; some were uncomfortably true. Then they turned each note into a rule. Exam weeks went on the calendar as break weeks. Every part got two owners, not one. They chose a small showcase for the class on the last Friday of each month, so there would always be something to look forward to. The terrace felt lighter afterwards.

qa.q: What did the team imagine had happened to the project by April?
qa.a: That it was dead, abandoned.

qa.q: What might Lakshmi feel while listing the ways the project could die?
qa.a: A little uneasy but relieved: saying the risks aloud made them feel manageable.

qa.q: What else could the team do to spot trouble early, and why?
qa.a: Hold a short weekly check-in to notice when interest or work starts to slip, since trouble is easier to fix early.

qa.q: How does the plan look to a team member who feared doing all the work?
qa.a: Two owners for every part is a relief, since the load is no longer that person's alone.

grounding: Before starting, a team imagines the project dead in two months, lists the reasons and adds exam breaks and shared ownership.

subtype: Approach: protecting privacy and safety while building [Action]
passage: “Devika, you asked how our class website avoided drama. I'm Asif, and I'll be honest, I almost skipped the boring part. We wanted photos of everyone. First I asked each classmate in person, and two said no. So those two appear as drawings we made together. The site shows first names only, no phone numbers, no school address, no class timetable. Before we published anything I showed the whole plan to our class teacher, who asked, ‘Who can see this?’ We changed it so only people with the link can open it, and the link goes through the class group, not the open internet. It took an extra week. But nobody woke up to find a stranger looking at their photo.”

qa.q: What names does the site show?
qa.a: First names only.

qa.q: What might Asif have been worried about while planning?
qa.a: That strangers might see classmates' photos and cause them harm or discomfort, which is why Asif asked everyone and showed the teacher.

qa.q: What else could Asif do to keep the site safe, and why?
qa.a: Check the site regularly and remove anything a classmate later wants taken down, since a person's consent can change.

qa.q: How does the plan look to a classmate who said no to a photo?
qa.a: That classmate feels respected because the refusal was accepted and a drawing was used instead.

grounding: A teen making a class website asks permission for photos, uses first names only and shows the plan to a teacher.

subtype: Approach: assuming visitors will just arrive [Pitfall]
passage: In the school entrepreneurship club room, Trisha ma'am scrolled through Varun's finished site: a small online store for hand-poured candles, with careful photos and a tidy checkout page. It had taken him two weekends. “How many visitors so far?” she asked. Varun turned his laptop. The counter read 4, after three weeks. “Those are all my own refreshes,” he admitted. “Who did you tell?” “Nobody. People will find it. It's online.” Trisha ma'am didn't lecture. “Who lives near you? Who is in this room?” Varun looked at the forty candles in the box under the table. His shoulders sank. He had spent hours on the site and not one minute on telling a single person it existed.

qa.q: What did the visitor counter show?
qa.a: Four, all from Varun's own refreshes.

qa.q: What might Varun feel as he looks at the counter?
qa.a: Deflated and puzzled: he built the store carefully and nobody came.

qa.q: What could Varun do instead, and why?
qa.a: Tell classmates, neighbours and local groups about the store with a short message and flyers, since nobody visits a site they do not know exists.

qa.q: How does the store look to a classmate who never heard of it?
qa.a: It does not exist for that classmate at all, because nobody told them about it.

grounding: After finishing a small online store, a student waits for traffic and none comes because nobody was told.

subtype: Approach: iterating from feedback and usage numbers [Revision]
passage: “Jasleen, sit down. I'll tell you how a number saved my school magazine site. I'm Kiran. I was sixteen and proud of it: four pages, and I'd put a little visit counter at the bottom, just for fun. After a month I looked. The home page had a hundred visits. The third page, my classmates' poetry, had two. Two! I was hurt. I asked my cousin why. My cousin said, ‘I never found it. It's hidden under More.’ I hadn't thought of that. I moved poetry to the front page, right under the title. Within a week it had thirty-one visits. The poems hadn't changed. Only where they sat.”

qa.q: How many visits did the poetry page get in the first month?
qa.a: Two.

qa.q: How did Kiran feel on learning why nobody opened the poetry page?
qa.a: Hurt at first, then surprised and a little embarrassed that the fault was the design and not the poems.

qa.q: Which choice in the story turned things around, and why?
qa.a: Asking why instead of guessing: the cousin's answer showed the page was hidden, so moving it to the front page fixed it.

qa.q: How might Kiran's cousin have felt when asked?
qa.a: The cousin was probably glad to be asked and to give honest feedback, and pleased to see the change made.

grounding: An elder recalls noticing from visit counts that nobody opened page three, asking why, moving it to the homepage and seeing visits rise.

subtype: Approach: deciding when to stop or hand over [Revision]
passage: “Lokesh, you asked how the handover happened, so here's the story. I ran the school events site for a year. In January I looked at my exam timetable and my to-do list, and I knew I couldn't do both. So I stopped adding features. I wrote a one-page note: how to add an event, where to find the photos, who to ask if something breaks, what not to touch. Then I gave it to you, and I put a banner across the top of the site: ‘Paused until April. New events will be added by Lokesh.’ It felt strange, almost like giving up a pet. But I'd rather say honestly it's paused than let it sit there quietly going out of date. — Payal

qa.q: What did Payal put across the top of the site?
qa.a: A banner saying it is paused until April, with new events added by Lokesh.

qa.q: How does Payal feel about handing over the site?
qa.a: Bittersweet: it felt like giving up a pet, but Payal was relieved not to let it go stale in silence.

qa.q: What else could Payal do to help the handover, and why?
qa.a: Do the first update together with Lokesh, since watching it done once makes the written notes easier to follow.

qa.q: How does the handover look to Lokesh?
qa.a: Lokesh receives a project with clear notes, though Lokesh may feel nervous about looking after something someone else built.

grounding: As board exams approach, a student freezes features, writes notes for a junior to maintain the site and pauses it honestly.
